title: Reading a tide table and a current table
teaches: Planning a beach walk at a minus tide and a crossing at slack water
summary: **A tide table lists the turns.** Each high and low, with its time and its height in feet above a fixed zero.
**Zero is the average lower low.** Mean lower low water (MLLW) is the average of each day's lower low over 19 years, so many lows fall below it.
**A minus tide is below that average.** On a flat low-tide terrace each foot below zero uncovers a strip of beach many metres wide.
**Charts use the same zero.** A charted depth plus the table's height gives the depth now, and is rarely less than the chart shows.
**The rule of twelfths estimates the height between turns.** In six equal parts of the time the water moves 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 and 1 twelfths of the range.
**A current table lists slack, maximum flood and maximum ebb.** Speeds are in knots, and one knot is about half a metre a second.
**Slack in a narrows comes after high water.** At Deception Pass it can be an hour or more late, so a crossing is planned from the current table.
**Slack in a fast pass is short.** Around the biggest slacks the water runs under a knot for well under an hour; in a slow inlet, for two hours or more.
**Seattle's daytime minus tides come from late spring to midsummer.** For a fixed hour, pick the day with the lowest water in that hour, not the lowest number in the week.

blocks.text: At Constellation Park, on the West Seattle shore just south of Alki Point, a broad shelf of rock and cobble runs out under the Sound. On most days the water covers its outer edge. On a few days each spring and summer the water draws back far enough to bare the whole shelf, and people walk out among the pools to find sea stars, anemones and crabs that spend nearly all their lives under water. Those days are known a year ahead, to the minute, from a table.

This lesson reads two tables that NOAA publishes for the Salish Sea and plans by them. The first target is a walk at a **minus tide**, at noon on a day you are free. The second is the moment the current under the Deception Pass bridge stops, which a different table gives. Lessons 8 to 11 explained why the water rises, falls and runs as it does. Here the tables do the predicting, and the skill is reading them.

blocks.caption: Where the tables apply in Seattle: the tide station on the downtown waterfront, and three beaches that uncover on the lowest tides.

blocks.text: NOAA's predictions for Seattle are computed from more than a century of records at its tide station on the downtown waterfront, station 9447130. Ask its website for a month of predictions and you get a list: for each day, the times of the highs and lows and how high each will be, in feet and in centimetres, each marked H or L.[^localtime] A late-May day reads something like this: 04:09 H 13.0, 11:22 L −2.1, 18:09 H 9.5, 23:03 L 5.2. The tables in this lesson's figures are made up but built the way NOAA builds its own, as a sum of regular waves (lesson 9), so they look like real ones. For a real walk, look up the real predictions.

Seattle's tide is mixed, as lesson 9 explained: two highs and two lows a day, of unequal size. The table shows it at a glance. The morning high is 13 feet, the evening high under 10, and one low is far below the other.

Every height is measured from a fixed zero called the **datum**. For tides in the United States the zero is **mean lower low water**, MLLW: take the lower of each day's two lows, over 19 years of them,[^epoch] and average them. So zero is not the bottom of the tide. It is an ordinary low, and on a good many days the lower low falls below it. Those are the minus tides, printed with a minus sign: −2.1 ft is 2.1 feet (64 cm) below the average lower low. At Seattle the average higher high stands about 11.4 ft (3.5 m) above zero, the biggest highs of the year reach 13 or 14 ft, and the lowest lows of the year fall about 3 to 4 ft below zero.

Why measure from an ordinary low and not from the middle? Because the same zero is used under the water. The depths on a nautical chart of Puget Sound are measured down from MLLW, so a sailor adds the table's height to the charted depth to get the depth now. With zero set near the low, the sum is seldom less than the chart shows, and when it is, the table warns with a minus sign.[^chart]

What a minus tide is worth depends on the beach. Many of the Sound's beaches have a steep upper part of gravel and cobble and, below it, a broad, nearly flat shelf, the **low-tide terrace**. While the tide falls across the steep part, the water's edge hardly moves. Once it falls across the terrace, every foot uncovers a wide strip.

blocks.caption: A model beach, with heights in feet above MLLW: a steep upper beach and a flat low-tide terrace. The bar at the bottom measures the beach uncovered beyond the average high-tide line.
blocks.task: Guess, then take the tide down to a minus tide

blocks.text: That is why people who walk the shore care about tenths of a foot below zero. Between a −1 ft and a −3 ft tide lies a strip of terrace tens of metres wide, and the animals that live on its outer edge are uncovered only on the few lowest tides of the year.

A tide table lists only the turns. Between them the water does not fall at an even pace. It starts slowly just after high water, runs fastest in the middle, and slows again as it nears the low, the way a swing slows at each end of its arc. Sailors estimate the height between the turns with the **rule of twelfths**: split the time from high to low into six equal parts, and in those parts the water falls 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 and 1 twelfths of the whole range.

Take Saturday's big fall in the made-up table: 13.0 ft at 04:09 to −2.1 ft at 11:22. The range is 15.1 ft, so a twelfth is about 1.26 ft. The time between is 7 hours 13 minutes, so a sixth is about 72 minutes. By 07:45, three sixths in, the water has fallen 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 twelfths, half the range, to about 5.5 ft. By 10:10, five sixths in, it has fallen 11 twelfths, to about −0.8 ft. The last 72 minutes bring only the final twelfth, a little over a foot.

blocks.caption: Saturday's tide in the model, the four entries of its table, and the rule of twelfths drawn between them.
blocks.task: Find the time when the water falls fastest

blocks.text: For a walk this matters in two ways. The water stays within about a foot of its lowest for an hour or more either side of the low, so arriving an hour early costs little. And the middle hours of the rising tide come back fast: on Saturday afternoon the water climbs more than a foot every half hour, over a terrace where a foot of height is many metres of beach.

The rule assumes a smooth, even tide. Seattle's is not quite that: its smaller rise and fall in the evening is lopsided, and there the rule drifts off by up to half a foot. For planning a walk that is close enough. For taking a deep boat over a shoal it is not, and NOAA also gives its predictions every six minutes for anyone who wants the curve itself.

A tide table says how high the water stands. A **current table** says how fast it moves, and which way, at one place: Deception Pass, Admiralty Inlet, the Tacoma Narrows, Rich Passage. For each day it lists the times of **slack water**, when the current stops and turns, and between each pair of slacks the time and speed of the strongest current: **maximum flood**, running in from the sea, and **maximum ebb**, running out. Speeds are in **knots**, nautical miles an hour.[^knot] One knot is about 1.85 km/h, or half a metre a second, a slow walk. Ebb speeds are often printed with a minus sign.

At Deception Pass the flood runs east, from Rosario Strait into Skagit Bay, and the ebb runs west. On the biggest tides the current there peaks at 6 to 8 knots, faster than a kayaker can paddle, and the water below the bridge breaks into whirlpools and standing waves. On an ordinary day it may peak at 4 or 5 knots. The water is moving almost all the time, and the table's slacks are short breaks in it.

Look at when the slacks come. Lesson 11 explained why, in a narrows, the current keeps running after the tide outside has turned: it follows the difference in level between the two sides, and the basin inside is still filling when the water outside has peaked. Slack at Deception Pass can come an hour or more after high water at the nearest tide station. A crossing planned from a tide table would meet the flood still running, which is why the two tables are published separately.

blocks.caption: Saturday in the model: the tide outside, the current it drives in a fast pass or a wide inlet, and the current table that results. Flood is up, ebb down; the shaded band is slower than 1 knot.
blocks.task: Guess, then find a slack in each channel

blocks.text: In a fast pass the slack is short. The current swings from about 7 knots one way to 7 knots the other in some six hours, so it passes through the slow speeds quickly, and around the biggest slacks it runs under a knot for well under an hour. In a wide inlet where the current peaks at 2 or 3 knots, the slow water lasts two hours or more. Divers, kayakers and boats with small engines plan around the slack windows of the passes and arrive early, since wind, air pressure and a river in flood can all move the real slack away from the predicted one.

**Watching it stop.** Look up the Deception Pass current predictions for a day with a big tide and stand on the bridge, which has walkways on both sides, at the time of maximum current. Then come back at the slack the table gives. The water that was boiling through the pass lies almost flat, and within half an hour it is moving the other way.

Back to the beach. Seattle's lowest tides come near the new and full moon (lesson 8), and the lower low of each day is deepest when the Moon stands far north or south of the equator (lesson 9). Which of those lows fall in daylight depends on the season. In late spring and early summer the lower low comes around the middle of the day; in winter, lows just as deep come in the middle of the night. So the year's best beach walks fall between about late April and July, in runs of several days around the new and full moons.

Within a run, the low comes later each day, by about 50 minutes on average, while its depth grows to a peak and shrinks again. The deepest low of the run is not always the best one. If your free hour is fixed, the day to pick is the one with the lowest water in that hour, and the rule of twelfths says how much a low an hour or two away has already risen.

blocks.caption: A made-up week of Seattle predictions in late May, built like real ones. Minus tides are in bold. The day's curve appears once you have guessed.
blocks.task: Guess from the table, then step through the week

blocks.text: Thursday has the week's lowest low, −2.7 ft, but at 09:55, and by noon the water is back to about zero. Friday's low is deeper than Saturday's but comes earlier, so by noon on Friday the water has risen more than a foot. Saturday's −2.1 ft at 11:22 leaves the water near −1.8 ft at noon, the lowest of the week in that hour.

Good places for a minus-tide walk in Seattle include Constellation Park and Lincoln Park in West Seattle and the North Beach of Discovery Park, below the bluffs north of West Point.[^subordinate] Each uncovers rock, sand and pools on the lowest tides that are under water most of the year. On the lowest summer tides, volunteer beach naturalists from the Seattle Aquarium are often there to show what lives on them.

The animals on the outer terrace are in the air for a few hours a year. Walk on bare rock and sand where you can, turn any rock you lift back the way it lay, and leave animals where you find them. Keep an eye on the time too: the flood comes back fastest in its middle hours, and over a flat terrace it can cross the sand behind you quicker than you expect and cut off an outer bar.

blocks.caption: Six questions on reading the tables
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A Seattle tide table lists a low of −2.5 ft. What does the minus sign mean?
choices: The water will stand 2.5 ft below the average of the daily lower lows, so more beach than usual is bare
The water will stand 2.5 ft below mean sea level, which is an ordinary low tide at Seattle
The tide will be falling at 2.5 ft an hour at that time, faster than on an ordinary day
items.why: Heights are measured from mean lower low water, the average of each day's lower low. A minus tide is lower than that average.

items.ask: Why is the zero of a US tide table set at the average lower low rather than at mean sea level?
choices: Charts measure depths from the same zero, so charted depth plus the table's height is seldom less than the chart shows
The lower low is the easiest level to see on a beach, so it was the first one surveyors could measure
Mean sea level changes every year, while the average lower low has stayed fixed since tide tables began
items.why: A low zero makes the depth on the chart a cautious figure: the water is usually deeper, and when it is shallower the table shows a minus height.

items.ask: High water is 12 ft at 06:00 and low water 0 ft at 12:00. By the rule of twelfths, about how high is the tide at 08:00?
choices: About 9 ft, since only 3 twelfths of the range fall in the first two of the six hours
About 8 ft, since the water falls an even 2 ft in each of the six hours
About 6 ft, since half of the fall comes in the first two hours after the turn
items.why: In the first two sixths the water falls 1 + 2 = 3 twelfths of 12 ft, so 3 ft, leaving about 9 ft. It falls slowly just after the turn.

items.ask: High water at the tide station nearest Deception Pass is at 10:40. When should a kayaker plan to go through the pass?
choices: At the slack time in the Deception Pass current table, which in a narrows often comes an hour or more after high water
At 10:40, since the current in a pass always stops at the moment of high water outside it
Half way between 10:40 and the next low water, when the tide is at mid-height and moving least
items.why: In a narrows the current follows the difference in level between the two sides, so it keeps running after high water outside. Only the current table gives the slack.

items.ask: Why does the water run slowly for a much shorter time around slack in Deception Pass than in a wide inlet with weak currents?
choices: The current swings from several knots one way to several knots the other in about six hours, so it passes the slow speeds quickly
The pass is narrow, so the water in it is pushed by the wind more than the water of a wide inlet
Slack in a pass happens only on the biggest tides, while in an inlet it happens on every tide
items.why: The faster the current at its peak, the faster it changes through zero. In the model, a 7 knot pass runs under 1 knot for well under an hour; a 2 to 3 knot inlet for two hours or more.

items.ask: Why are late spring and early summer the season for minus-tide walks at Seattle?
choices: Then the day's lower low falls around midday; in winter, lows just as deep come at night
Then the Moon is closest to the Earth, so the only minus tides of the year happen in those months
Then the rivers carry the least water into the Sound, so the sea surface stands lowest
items.why: Deep lows happen all year, but which of the two daily lows is the lower one, and when it falls, changes with the season. In summer it is the daytime low.

localtime.title: Clock time
localtime.text: NOAA's tables can be printed in standard time or in local time. Choose local time (LST/LDT). In summer a table in standard time has every entry an hour away from the clock on your phone.

epoch.title: Why 19 years
epoch.text: The tilt of the Moon's orbit to the Earth's equator swings through a cycle of 18.6 years, and the sizes of the tides swing with it. Averaging over a whole cycle makes the zero the same whichever years are chosen, apart from changes in sea level itself. As the sea rises NOAA recomputes its datums from a newer run of years, so zero on the table moves slightly from one recomputation to the next.

chart.title: Other zeros
chart.text: Not every country uses the average lower low. British charts use the lowest astronomical tide, about the lowest level the tide reaches in ordinary weather, so a minus height almost never appears. Canadian charts of the Salish Sea use a low datum of their own, so a Canadian and an American table for nearby places can give different numbers for the same water.

knot.title: The knot
knot.text: Sailors once measured speed by throwing a wooden board over the stern on a line with knots tied in it at even spacings, and counting how many knots ran out while a small sandglass emptied. The spacing and the glass were matched so that the count gave nautical miles an hour. A nautical mile is 1,852 m, about one minute of latitude.

subordinate.title: Beaches without a station
subordinate.text: NOAA keeps long-running tide stations at a few places, such as Seattle and Port Townsend, and gives many more places as differences from one of them: add so many minutes to the times and scale the heights by so much. For a beach a few miles from the Seattle station the differences are small, so the Seattle table serves well.
